title: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR)
hook: Keyword search misses answers that use different words. DPR embeds questions and passages into one vector space and retrieves by meaning — the backbone of modern vector search.
key_points: Embeds questions and passages into a shared vector space.
Retrieves by nearest-neighbor similarity, not keyword overlap.
Two encoders are trained so a question lands near its answer passage.
Beat strong keyword baselines like BM25 on open-domain question answering.
Learned dense retrieval became the foundation of vector search in RAG.
content_html: DPR, from Karpukhin, Oğuz, and colleagues at Facebook AI in 2020, learns to retrieve text by meaning rather than matching words. It encodes questions and passages into the same vector space so a question sits near the passages that answer it, and you retrieve via nearest-neighbor search. This learned dense approach beat strong keyword baselines on open-domain question answering.
extra_html:
How it works

DPR uses two encoders — one for questions, one for passages — that map text to dense vectors. During training, the model pulls a question's vector close to its correct passage and pushes it away from irrelevant ones (using in-batch negatives). At query time you embed the question and find the closest passage vectors with fast nearest-neighbor search over a precomputed index.

Why it matters

Keyword search fails when the answer phrases things differently from the question. By matching on learned meaning instead, DPR retrieves relevant passages that lexical search would miss, improving downstream answers. The question-and-passage encoder setup plus vector nearest-neighbor lookup is exactly the retrieval engine inside most RAG systems today.

related.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
related.hook: Why force a model to memorize everything? RAG lets it look things up — fetch relevant documents, then answer from that evidence instead of frozen weights alone.
